documents.title: Outside ED Record (received)
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Regional hospital Emergency Department. Date of service 05/07/2025.

CC: trouble breathing, drooling, belly cramps.

HPI: 40M farmer who applies pesticide for his own crops. Was out spraying a field earlier today and started feeling sick while working. Wife drove him in; she says he has been drenched in sweat and not making sense. Arrives with difficulty breathing, excessive salivation and cramping abdominal pain.

PMH: none. PSH: tonsillectomy as a child (age 8). Meds: none. Allergies: NKDA.
FH: father HTN dx at 65, mother hypothyroid. No neuro or psych illness in the family.
SH: never smoker, 2-3 drinks/month, crop farmer / ag pesticide applicator.

Triage VS: RR 28, HR 110, BP 135/85, T 37.2 C.

Exam: Tachypneic, wet. Pupils miotic. Fasciculations diffusely over trunk and limbs. Expiratory wheeze throughout. Skin moist. Distinct garlic odor on him and his clothes. Abdomen soft.

ABG on arrival: pH 7.30 / pCO2 50 / pO2 60.

MDM: Cholinergic toxidrome after organophosphate exposure, with bronchorrhea, bronchospasm and hypoventilation. Staff in gowns and gloves; clothes bagged, skin washed down. Non-rebreather on. Atropine IV in doubling boluses until secretions dried and wheeze cleared, then started on drip. Pralidoxime 2 g IV load, then infusion. Repeat gas after atropinization pH 7.39 / pCO2 41 / pO2 88 on 2 L. Did not need airway. Plasma cholinesterase sent.

Dx: Organophosphate poisoning, accidental.
Dispo: admit MICU.

documents.title: Outside Discharge Summary (received)
documents.author: critical care
documents.body:
Regional hospital, Medical Intensive Care Unit
Admitted 05/07/2025  Discharged 05/10/2025

Diagnosis: Organophosphate poisoning (accidental occupational exposure while spraying crops).

Hospital course: Admitted from the ED after decontamination, atropine boluses and a pralidoxime load. Plasma cholinesterase on arrival 1,050 U/L (ref 5,320-12,920). Continued on atropine infusion with titration to dry lungs and secretions, and pralidoxime infusion. Oxygen weaned from non-rebreather to nasal cannula to room air over the first day. No intubation. Atropine off hospital day 2 without return of secretions; pralidoxime stopped day 3. Mental status back to baseline by the morning after admission. No arrhythmia on telemetry. Tolerating diet, walking the unit without difficulty at discharge.

Discharge medications: none.
Allergies: NKDA.

Instructions: no handling of pesticides until a repeat cholinesterase has recovered. Wash and set aside any contaminated clothing; do not launder with household laundry. Patient does not have a primary care physician; advised to establish care and be seen within 2 weeks for a repeat cholinesterase level.

Copy to: patient's new primary care office on request.

documents.title: Outside Records Received
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Hospital records for 5/7-5/10 admission came in by fax this morning (ED record + discharge summary, labs). Scanned and sent to PCP ahead of his new patient visit tomorrow.

documents.title: New Patient Call
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Christopher called, wants to become a patient here. Just home from the hospital Saturday after a pesticide exposure, discharge paperwork says to see a PCP within 2 weeks. Hasn't had a regular doctor since he was a kid. Booked new patient visit 5/21 at 8:30. Emailed records release for the hospital, he signed and returned it before we hung up. Request faxed to their medical records dept.

documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
NEW PATIENT / HOSPITAL FOLLOW-UP

40 y/o man establishing care, 11 days out from a 3-night ICU stay for organophosphate poisoning. Hospital records reviewed (received yesterday).

He was spraying his own field on 5/7 and got sick partway through: short of breath, drooling, cramping. Wife took him in. Treated with decontamination, atropine and pralidoxime, never intubated, home on 5/10 on nothing. Since then he says he feels essentially back to himself. Tired the first few days, now gone. No cough, no wheeze, no shortness of breath on the farm chores he's been doing. No twitching, no weakness in his arms or legs, no trouble swallowing, no blurry vision, no diarrhea or cramps. Sleeping fine. Has not touched the sprayer since.

Mixes and applies for his own acreage and holds an applicator license. Not sure exactly how he got the exposure that day.

PMH: nothing chronic. No regular doctor since childhood.
PSH: tonsillectomy at 8.
Meds: none. Allergies: NKDA.
FH: father with hypertension, diagnosed at 65. Mother hypothyroid. No neurologic or psychiatric illness in the family.
SH: married, lives in Easthampton. Never smoker. Alcohol 2-3 drinks a month. Works the farm with his brother.
PHQ-2: 0.

Exam: well-appearing, comfortable. Pupils equal, normal size, reactive. Oropharynx moist, not excessively so. Lungs clear, no wheeze, good air movement. Heart regular, no murmur. Abdomen soft, nontender, normal bowel sounds. No fasciculations at rest. Strength 5/5 proximally and distally including neck flexion. Reflexes 2+ and symmetric. Gait normal. Skin intact, no rash.

A/P:
1. Organophosphate poisoning, recovering. Clinically back to baseline. Cholinesterase today to see how far it has come back from 1,050 in the hospital. No mixing or spraying until it's in the normal range; brother can cover. When he does go back: chemical-resistant coveralls, gloves and boots, a properly fitted respirator per the product label, change and wash immediately after any splash, and keep work clothes out of the family wash. Reviewed what early symptoms to stop work for (sweating, drooling, cramping, blurred vision, twitching) and to get to an ED rather than waiting it out.
2. Health maintenance: CBC, CMP, lipids, A1c today; one-time HIV and hep C screen, he agrees. Tdap status unknown, will plan with fall vaccines. Colon screening at 45.

Follow up by portal with results; recheck cholinesterase in about a month.

documents.title: Lab Results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Hi Christopher,

Your routine labs from Wednesday are all normal: blood count, kidney and liver tests, sugar (A1c). Cholesterol is fine for your age and risk, nothing to treat. HIV and hepatitis C screens were negative.

The cholinesterase level has come up a long way, from 1,050 in the hospital to 4,400, but it isn't in the normal range yet (normal starts a little above 5,300). That fits with how the body recovers after this kind of exposure, which takes weeks. So for now, please keep off the sprayer and away from mixing. I've put in an order to recheck it in about a month; you can stop by the lab any morning after 6/23.

Glad you're feeling well.

documents.title: RE: Lab Results
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Ok thanks. My brother is doing the spraying for now. Will come in end of June.

documents.title: Cholinesterase Recheck
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Christopher, your cholinesterase is now 7,600, back in the normal range. You're cleared to go back to mixing and spraying, with the full protective gear we talked about every time: coveralls, chemical gloves and boots, and the respirator the label calls for. Change right away if anything splashes on you. If you ever start sweating, drooling, cramping or twitching while working, stop and get to the ED.

documents.title: Immunizations
documents.author: RN
documents.body: In after harvest work for vaccines. No record of a tetanus booster he can remember; Tdap given per PCP plan. Flu (trivalent) L deltoid, Moderna 2025-26 R deltoid, Tdap R deltoid. No prior vaccine reactions. Waited 15 min, felt fine, left.

documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Pt left vm at 7:10, needs to cancel his physical for tomorrow 4/8, getting fields ready and can't get away. Called back, he'll call to rebook once planting is done. Visit cancelled.

documents.title: Outside ED Record (received)
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Regional hospital Emergency Department. DOS 05/07/2026.

CC: collapse.

HPI: 41M, known to us from an ICU stay a year ago for organophosphate poisoning with breathing trouble, salivation and cramps. Brother brought him in from the farm after he went down suddenly while working. Per brother he had been spraying crops all day with no protective gear, and slopped some of the concentrate on his shirt but kept going. Product had a strong, bitter smell. First complained of feeling dizzy and sick to his stomach and said his vision was off. Over a few minutes he was pouring sweat, cramping and vomiting, then got confused, stumbled more than once, and had a short generalized seizure that stopped by itself before EMS was needed. Brother reports nobody else working there today is sick.

Meds: none. NKDA.

Arrival VS: HR 56, BP 104/62, RR 24, SpO2 89% RA, T 36.6 C.

Exam: On the stretcher drooling, mumbling and not making sense. Shirt and pants soaked with sweat. Tremulous. Shallow respirations, intermittent cough bringing up small amounts of clear sputum. Pupils pinpoint, sluggish to light. Skin cool and clammy. Fasciculations in both arms and both legs. Abdomen not distended, nontender, bowel sounds hyperactive.

MDM: Recurrent cholinergic crisis from organophosphate exposure. Clothes removed and bagged, washed down. Oxygen by NRB. Atropine IV boluses titrated to dry secretions, then infusion. Pralidoxime 2 g IV load and infusion. No further seizure activity. Airway protected on his own, no intubation. Plasma cholinesterase sent.

Dx: Organophosphate poisoning, accidental, recurrent. Seizure attributed to the poisoning.
Dispo: MICU.

documents.title: Outside Discharge Summary (received)
documents.author: critical care
documents.body:
Regional hospital, Medical Intensive Care Unit
Admitted 05/07/2026  Discharged 05/09/2026

Principal diagnosis: Organophosphate poisoning, accidental occupational exposure (second episode; prior ICU admission 05/2025).

Course: Arrived after collapse with a single self-limited generalized convulsion in the field. Cholinesterase on arrival 820 U/L (ref 5,320-12,920). Decontaminated in the ED and treated with atropine boluses and infusion plus pralidoxime load and infusion. Observed two nights in the unit. Off oxygen within the first day. No recurrent convulsion. Atropine and pralidoxime weaned off without return of cholinergic signs. Alert and oriented, eating, ambulating independently at discharge.

Discharge meds: none. Allergies: NKDA.

Follow-up: PCP within 1 week with repeat cholinesterase. No pesticide handling until cleared. Discussed protective equipment at length with patient and brother.

cc: PCP of record.

documents.title: Post-Discharge Call
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Called pt after Saturday discharge (ICU 5/7-5/9, pesticide exposure again). Says he's tired and a little sore but otherwise ok. No more seizures, no drooling or sweating spells, breathing fine, eating normally. Wife is with him; he is not driving yet. Not on any meds. Hospital paperwork says PCP within a week + cholinesterase. Booked Thu 5/14 at 9:00. Asked him to stay away from the sprayer and the chemical shed until then. Records requested from hospital.

documents.title: Hospital Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
HOSPITAL FOLLOW-UP

Seen 5 days after discharge from a 2-night ICU stay for a second organophosphate poisoning, a year after the first. Hospital ED record and discharge summary reviewed.

He was spraying without any protective gear on 5/7 and spilled some on his shirt. Collapsed in the field, one brief generalized seizure that stopped on its own, brother drove him in. Treated with atropine and pralidoxime, no intubation, cholinesterase 820 on arrival. Home 5/9 on nothing.

Today: energy coming back, still naps in the afternoon. No further seizure or spells, no twitching, no drooling or sweats, no cramping, vision normal, breathing normal. Hasn't driven. Has not been near the chemicals since.

We talked about how this happened. He knows he skipped the gear that day and was in a hurry to get the field done. Wife and brother have both been on him about it.

Meds: none. NKDA.

Exam: alert, conversant, looks well. Pupils 4 mm, equal and briskly reactive. Mouth not wet. Lungs clear. Heart regular. Abdomen soft, nontender, normal bowel sounds. No fasciculations. Strength full throughout including neck flexors and hip flexors. Reflexes symmetric. Gait and tandem normal. Speech and thinking normal.

A/P:
Organophosphate poisoning, second episode, recovering. Cholinesterase today. No mixing, loading or spraying until it is back to normal. The convulsion happened with the poisoning and has not recurred. Went over the protective equipment again in detail: coveralls, chemical-resistant gloves and boots, eye protection and the respirator the label requires, every load, every time; change and wash at once after a splash; contaminated clothing bagged and kept out of the house laundry. Brother will run the sprayer for now. He knows the early symptoms and to stop work and go to the ED if they start.

Result by portal. Recheck cholinesterase in about a month. Physical to be rebooked.

results.test: Cholinesterase [Enzymatic activity/volume] in Serum or Plasma

documents.title: Cholinesterase Result
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Christopher, today's cholinesterase is 7,400, normal again (it was 3,900 at your visit in May). Your body has recovered from the exposure.

documents.title: Back to work?
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Saw the result. Does that mean I can go back to spraying? Bought a new respirator and suit.

documents.title: RE: Back to work?
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Yes, from a medical standpoint you can go back to it, with the new suit and respirator on for every load, plus gloves, boots and eye protection. Change right away after any splash. Two episodes is a pattern I don't want to see a third time, so please don't skip the gear even for a quick job. Stop and go to the ED at the first sign of sweating, drooling, cramps, blurry vision or twitching.

documents.title: Physical
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Need to reschedule the physical I cancelled back in April. Mornings are best, anytime after Labor Day.

documents.title: RE: Physical
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Hi Christopher, you're booked for Wednesday 9/16 at 8:00 am with the doctor. Reply here if that doesn't work.
